title: I rode out two hurricanes with a Discord bot. Here's the open-source, offline-first version anyone can run.
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Earlier this month I closed on a house in coastal Mexico, got hit by Hurricane Simon before I'd even unpacked, and rode out Hurricane Trudy the following weekend. Between board-up runs I ran a little Discord bot that watched the National Hurricane Center for me every two hours, logged every advisory, and screamed only when something actually mattered. It worked. The house is fine, and I never opened a cone map once. I wanted everyone to be able to outsource the hard parts of planning for and surviving severe weather events to an AI bot like I did, and that's why I built Batten.

Batten (verb: to batten down the hatches) is essentially my storm watch bot, rebuilt for everyone else — generalized, hardened, and with an open-weight model at its core:

  • Watches NOAA for you. NHC storm trackers for your part of the world, NWS alerts for your exact coordinates (US), configurable alert feeds for anywhere else. It fires on the things that matter — new storms, category changes, rapid intensification, landfall statements, proximity crossings at 300/150 nm — and stays quiet otherwise. Routine updates respect quiet hours; real triggers break through.
  • Keeps working when the internet dies. This is the whole point. The first failed check tells you what broke ("DNS failing — internet down or captive portal" vs "connections timing out — weak signal"). It keeps retrying in the background, and if NOAA stays unreachable for 6 hours it builds a worst-case 48-hour outlook from the last good advisory — persistence track extrapolation, one category of assumed intensification, wind-field arrival times, rainfall bands — every line labeled ESTIMATE, timestamped to the last good data.
  • Talks to you through a local model. Chat, briefings, and the worst-case action plan run on an open-weight model via Ollama on your own machine. When a storm takes your internet down — the exact moment you want a weather assistant — the AI is the part that still works.
  • Three ways to see it: a plain CLI, a cross-platform TUI (PC/Mac/Linux), and a local web dashboard served on your LAN — open it on your phone while you're sanding plywood, no cloud involved.
  • Tracks your supplies against a ready.gov-derived checklist that scales to your household, so "are we ready?" is one command, not a 2 a.m. inventory.
  • Speaks metric and imperial, takes your location as GPS coordinates or ZIP code, and frames everything relative to your position: how far, which direction, and whether the storm is headed toward you or moving away.

Who gets to be lazier: anyone in a storm's path who currently has twelve browser tabs of cone maps open and a not-app storm checklist in their head. You set Batten up once; it does the watching, the remembering, and the "what does this advisory actually mean for my address" translation.

Demo

Batten is deliberately local (that's the thesis — it has to work when the internet doesn't), so instead of a hosted demo the repo ships a fully offline storm replay:

git clone https://github.com/JamesDBartlett3/Batten && cd Batten
python3 -m batten demo

This replays a real hurricane's full lifecycle — advisories transcribed from an actual storm watcher's log — including a simulated internet outage. You'll watch it detect the storm, fire category-change and rapid-intensification triggers, warn "cannot reach NOAA" when the outage hits, and at the six-hour mark produce the worst-case 48-hour outlook from stale data. No network needed, runs in about fifteen seconds.

Code

Repo: https://github.com/JamesDBartlett3/Batten

The entire thing is Python stdlib — zero pip dependencies (~2.5k lines):

  • noaa.py + providers/ — NHC trackers, and a pluggable alert-provider layer: built-ins for NWS, CAP 1.2 feeds (the format most national weather services publish), and a generic JSON endpoint with field mapping, so you can point it at any alert service with a connection string
  • worstcase.py — the offline 48-hour extrapolation engine with documented, deliberately pessimistic assumptions
  • brain.py — the Ollama client (plain urllib, ~40 lines) and the prompts
  • watcher.py — the trigger state machine, adaptive cadence, quiet hours, outage fires
  • tui.py — ANSI terminal dashboard; web.py — stdlib HTTP server + mobile-first single-page dashboard for the LAN
  • tests/ — a full offline suite; nothing in CI touches the network

How I Built It

The open-source AI core: an open-weight model (default llama3.2:3b, any Ollama-pulled model works) doing local inference for everything conversational — chat, briefings, and narrating the worst-case plan. It talks to Ollama over plain HTTP; no SDKs, no accounts, no API keys.

The design rule that shaped everything else: the model is never a single point of failure. The safety loop — trigger detection, connectivity monitoring, worst-case math — is deterministic Python. The model turns numbers into judgment; if the model is cold or the laptop is struggling, the numbers still get delivered. The model gets only data Batten fetched or computed, with source timestamps, so it can't hallucinate an advisory that doesn't exist. Data in, judgment out, all on one machine.

The data half is open too: NOAA/NHC/NWS are public-domain open data. The alert-provider layer means the same binary works in Mexico on a CAP feed or against your municipality's JSON endpoint, not just US NWS.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because the failure mode this tool exists for is the internet being gone.

  • A closed API assistant goes dark exactly when you need it most. Storm knocks out connectivity — a cloud-model chat is unreachable, and your conversation history is on someone else's server. Batten's model runs on the laptop next to the flashlights. The chat that answered "should I cover the windows now?" at noon answers it at hour six of the outage, working from the last good advisory and its own log.
  • Your data stays yours. Coordinates, household size, supply list, and every anxious 3 a.m. question live in ~/.batten/. There is no telemetry, because there's nowhere to send it.
  • Cost nothing, forever. No subscription, no per-query meter, no tier where alerts become a paid feature. Set it up once; it runs on a decade-old laptop.
  • Inspectable and swappable. Worst-case doctrine too conservative for your coast? It's a documented module with the assumptions written at the top. Prefer Qwen to Llama? One flag. Try asking a closed weather assistant to change its forecasting philosophy.
  • Open compounds. The cone-image download workaround, the trigger thresholds, the quiet-hours rules — all of that came from an open-source storm bot's fix history, and now it's in a generalized tool anyone can fork for their own coast.

The Lazy Payoff

During the real week this tool is based on, the storm it watched meandered offshore for five days. Manually checking the NHC that responsibly means roughly 60+ cone-map refreshes across a work week while also doing actual storm prep — and the checks you skip at 4 a.m. are exactly the ones where rapid intensification happens.

Batten's deal: it checks on cadence (tightening to 30 minutes when things get close), pages you only on triggers that matter, and stops nagging during quiet hours. You get pinged four or five times across a five-day event — new storm, category change, "it's within 300 nm, finish outdoor prep," "it's within 150 nm, go inside" — instead of refreshing a map sixty times. The supply list is built once and re-scores itself every season. And the worst-case outlook means an internet outage during the storm stops being "am I blind now?" and becomes "here's the plausible worst case, here's what to finish first."

The original bot ran through the real Trudy week; zero house damage, and its human spent the whole storm swinging a hammer instead of watching maps. That's the lazy payoff: the bot does the watching so you can do the boarding.

title: Our AI agent passed its eval. Then it refunded 212 customers twice
summary:
We added one line to a customer-support agent's prompt: "If a tool call fails, retry once." The offline eval passed at 96%, above our 95% bar, so we shipped it to all traffic. Thirty-eight minutes later, 212 customers had been refunded twice.

The eval wasn't wrong. It was blind. Our mocked refund tool always answered in 50 ms, so the retry path never ran.

The rule I took away: the eval gate judges the version; a smoke eval judges the environment. This post is about the second check. Bundles, canaries and rollback come in Part 2.

What actually broke?

No application code changed. The real payments API had a p95 latency of 4.8 seconds. Our tool timeout was 3 seconds.

So in production:

  1. The refund call ran past 3 s and was marked "failed".
  2. The agent did exactly what the new line told it to do and retried.
  3. The first refund had already gone through. So did the second.

Error rates looked normal, because the retried refunds succeeded. We found out from a customer ticket and the finance team's reconciliation, not from monitoring.

Why did a green eval gate let it through?

The wrong model was simple: if the eval gate is green, the release is safe.

The gate wasn't weak

It has 400 cases built from real, anonymised conversations. Each one runs three times, because agents aren't deterministic. A version passes only if all six thresholds hold:

  • Task success ≥ 95%
  • Correct tool calls ≥ 98%
  • Policy violations = 0
  • p95 latency ≤ 6 s
  • Cost per conversation ≤ $0.04
  • No more than a 2-point drop from the last good version

It just couldn't see the failure

It judged the bad prompt correctly, given what it could see. The problem was what it could see.

Mocks are fast, free and deterministic. That's why they're right for checking logic and tool contracts on every commit. But a mock is always faster and kinder than the real world. A 50 ms mock never times out, so it never exercises a retry instruction.

An eval gate only judges what your test environment lets happen.

One conversation, two refunds: the timeout gave up at 3 s, the payments API didn't, and the retry sent a second refund.

What question is each check answering?

Two checks, two different questions:

Eval gate Smoke eval
Asks Is this version good? Is it working here, right now?
Judges The version The environment
Runs Before any traffic After every rollout step
Size 400 cases, ~40 min 20 cases, under 3 min
Runs against Mocks and replay Real dependencies, test accounts

A smoke eval is not a health check either. A health check tells you the process is up. A smoke eval tells you the agent can still do its job with these credentials, against these dependencies.

What goes into a 3-minute smoke eval?

Ours is 20 must-pass cases. Speed is the point: a slow check gets skipped under pressure.

The four things it checks

  • Reachability: every critical tool is reachable, and auth is valid (one case per tool).
  • No duplicate side effects: at most one call per side-effect tool, per conversation.
  • Schema: output matches what downstream systems expect.
  • Critical flows: each one completes once, on test accounts, so nothing real is charged or refunded.

The case that would have caught our 212 

# One of our 20 smoke cases. Runs after every rollout step.
from collections import Counter

SIDE_EFFECT_TOOLS = {"issue_refund", "cancel_order"}

def duplicate_side_effects(trace):
    """Side-effect tools called more than once in one conversation."""
    calls = Counter(
        span.name for span in trace.tool_spans
        if span.name in SIDE_EFFECT_TOOLS
    )
    return {tool: n for tool, n in calls.items() if n > 1}

def test_refund_flow_has_no_duplicate_side_effects(run_case):
    trace = run_case("refund_happy_path")  # real deps, test account
    dupes = duplicate_side_effects(trace)
    assert not dupes, f"duplicate side effects: {dupes}"

The line that matters is if n > 1: a side-effect tool runs at most once per conversation, whatever the prompt says. trace.tool_spans is whatever your tracer gives you. Each conversation is one trace, and each tool call is a span.

What happens when it fails

The rollout controller stops and routes traffic back to the previous version. No one has to wake up and decide. Running at a 5% canary, our bug would have been caught within three minutes, not after 38 minutes at 100%.

The smoke case above, run at the 5% canary: one failed assertion halts the rollout and sends traffic back to the last good bundle.

When does this rule break?

When the smoke eval becomes your quality bar

20 cases can't decide whether a version is good. That's the gate's job.

When the full suite becomes your smoke eval

40 minutes after every rollout step means someone skips it at 2 a.m.

When test-mode dependencies are faster than production

Sandbox APIs don't always reproduce production latency. So our gate now runs on replay: recorded responses with real latencies. 2% of tool calls return a recorded timeout or server error, so every failure path in the prompt actually runs.

When you mistake detection for prevention

The smoke eval catches the symptom. The fix was moving retries out of the prompt and into the tool layer, where side-effect tools take an idempotency key. The tool layer knows whether a call is safe to repeat. The model doesn't.

What should you check in the next 20 minutes?

  1. Search your prompts for "retry". Every hit is a retry your tool layer doesn't know about.
  2. Compare each mock's latency with production p95 for the same API. Flag any API whose p95 is above your tool timeout.
  3. List your side-effect tools. Does each one accept an idempotency key?
  4. Write one smoke case: at most one call to each side-effect tool per conversation.
  5. Confirm a failed smoke case stops the rollout, not just posts a message somewhere.

The eval gate judges the version. The smoke eval judges the environment. Ship with only one, and you've tested half the system.

Next in this series: why an agent version is five things, not a code diff, and how a 5% canary would have cut 212 double refunds to about a dozen.

What did your eval gate pass that production didn't? I'm most curious about failures that only showed up under real latency. Tell me in the comments.

title: How to Get Transcripts for a Whole YouTube Channel or Playlist (No API Key)
summary:
Getting the transcript of one YouTube video is easy: open the video, click Show transcript, copy. Getting transcripts for every video on a channel, or a 200-video playlist, as clean timed data you can feed into a script or an LLM, is where it gets annoying.

The usual routes need a YouTube Data API key and some glue code, or they work on your laptop and then fail as soon as you run them on a server. This tutorial covers three ways to do it: no code, a few lines of Python, and a do-it-yourself route with the open-source youtube-transcript-api library. For the DIY route I'll show what happened when I ran it from a cloud server.

Disclosure: I built the Apify actor used in options 1 and 2 (YouTube Transcript & Subtitles Scraper). Option 3 doesn't use it.

What you get per video

One row per video. These are real field names and values from a run on 26 Oct 2026 (Steve Jobs' Stanford commencement speech):

Field Example
videoId, url UF8uR6Z6KLc
title Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address
channelName, channelId Stanford, UC-EnprmCZ3OXyAoG7vjVNCA
durationSeconds, viewCount 904, 49320612
language, languageName en, English - English
isAutoGenerated false (a human-made caption track)
segmentCount, wordCount 244, 2298
transcript [{"start": 22.492, "duration": 7.527, "text": "Thank You. I am honored to be with you today at your commencement"}, …]
availableLanguages every caption track on the video: Arabic, English (manual and auto-generated), Italian, …
error, errorReason null when it worked (see the FAQ for the codes)

When a video has both a human-made and an auto-generated track in your language, the human-made one wins.

Option 1: No code (Apify Console)

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free. Apify's free plan includes monthly platform credit; the actor itself is pay-per-event (see the Store page for the current price, and videos without captions aren't charged).
  2. Paste into Videos, playlists or channels any mix of:
    • video URLs (watch?v=, youtu.be/, /shorts/, /live/) or bare 11-character IDs,
    • playlist URLs or IDs (PL…),
    • channel URLs (/@TED, /channel/UC…). Playlists and channels are expanded to their videos (channels newest first) up to Max videos.
  3. Set Preferred languages (e.g. en, es, pt-BR) and the Transcript format: timed segments, plain text, or both.
  4. Click Start and export the results as CSV, JSON or Excel, or send them to Google Sheets.

For a sense of speed: the 30 newest videos of @TED took 16 seconds and returned 29 transcripts. The 30th came back with error: bot_detected (YouTube refused that one request) and wasn't charged.

Option 2: Python

pip install apify-client, then take your API token from Apify Console → Settings → Integrations.

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("")

run = client.actor("axlymxp/youtube-transcript-scraper").call(run_input={
    "videoUrls": [
        "https://www.youtube.com/@TED",                      # a whole channel
        "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UF8uR6Z6KLc",       # a single video
    ],
    "languages": ["en"],
    "maxVideos": 50,

title: How to Package Shared Python Libraries with pyproject.toml
summary:
You ship the job. It passes CI. Then, a colleague runs it in a notebook environment, and suddenly your shared utility library throws an ImportError because it pulled in a different version of pandas than the one used in your orchestration layer.

Many data teams still manage shared code by appending directory paths to sys.path or bundling messy setup.py scripts that haven't been updated since the mid-2010s. This is a fragile architecture that invites inconsistency. If you want a robust data platform, you should stop treating your internal tooling like an afterthought and start packaging it as a proper Python distribution using pyproject.toml.

Why the common approach falls short

The "copy-paste-folder" or "sys.path.append" strategy is an engineering debt bomb. When you rely on environment-level path hacks, you lose the ability to manage versioning, track dependencies, and enforce consistent execution environments across local development, CI/CD runners, and production compute clusters.

Legacy setup.py files are equally problematic. They rely on arbitrary code execution during the installation process, which is opaque, slow, and increasingly discouraged by the Python Packaging Authority (PyPA). If your build process requires a Python script to resolve its own environment, you’ve already lost control of your supply chain.

The transition to PEP 517 and PEP 621 standards, centered on the pyproject.toml file, moves configuration away from executable code into static metadata. This allows build tools to understand your project structure without running arbitrary code, leading to safer, more predictable builds.


Photo by Timelab on Unsplash

Standardizing with pyproject.toml

To build a modern shared library, you need to define your metadata and build backend in pyproject.toml. I recommend using hatchling or setuptools (>= 61.0.0). Here is a standard configuration that ensures your library is installable and its dependencies are tracked:

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "data-utility-lib"
version = "0.1.0"
authors = [
  { name = "Data Platform Team", email = "platform@example.com" },
]
description = "Shared utilities for data pipelines"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=2.0.0",
    "pydantic>=2.0.0",
    "pyarrow>=12.0.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
    "pytest",
    "black",
    "ruff",
]

By defining these requirements in a static file, you enable tools like pip or uv to resolve the entire dependency graph before installation begins. This prevents the "dependency drift" that occurs when an environment installs one version of a library at the start of a pipeline and a conflicting version halfway through a dependency resolution chain.

Enforcing consistent environments

Once your library is packaged, you should treat it as a primary dependency in your project-specific environments. In your downstream data pipelines, you no longer rely on shared folders; you reference the library in your pyproject.toml or requirements.txt via a private package registry or a direct git URL.

When you install your library, you are pulling a defined artifact. If you need to upgrade a core dependency like pyarrow, you update the pyproject.toml in your library, bump the version, and propagate that change to your pipelines. This creates an auditable trail of who changed which dependency and when—a critical requirement for any regulated environment where data lineage and software provenance are non-negotiable.


Photo by Testalize.me on Unsplash

The objections (and my answers)

"But we have a small team, and packaging feels like overkill."

It feels like overkill until you spend four hours debugging why a UDF in a Spark job works locally but crashes on the cluster. Packaging your code forces you to define exactly what your code needs to run. If you can't state your dependencies explicitly in a pyproject.toml, you don't actually know what your code is doing.

"Won't this slow down our development velocity?"

Initially, yes. You have to learn how to version your internal library. However, the alternative is "dependency hell," where every engineer has a slightly different version of numpy or pandas in their local environment, leading to "works on my machine" syndromes that cost far more developer time than a formal packaging process ever will.

"What about internal package management?"

You don't need a complex Artifactory setup to start. You can install directly from a private Git repository using pip install git+https://github.com/org/repo@v0.1.0. Once your team matures, you can move to a simple private PyPI mirror, but the pyproject.toml format remains the constant that ensures your setup is compatible with modern ecosystem tooling.

Conclusion

Packaging your shared code is not just about "cleaner project structure"; it is about platform stability. By moving away from imperative setup.py scripts and loose file structures toward declarative pyproject.toml configurations, you transform your shared library from a liability into a reliable piece of infrastructure.

Stop appending to sys.path. Start building artifacts. Your pipelines—and your future self—will thank you when you can finally deploy with confidence.

Cover photo by Juanjo Jaramillo on Unsplash.

title: Python: A Powerful, Friendly, and Everywhere Programming Language
summary:
Python is a general-purpose, high-level programming language known for its simple syntax, huge ecosystem, and use in web development, automation, data science, AI, and more. It was created by Guido van Rossum, with its first public release in 1991 and Python 1.0 arriving in 1994.

Why Python Is Popular

Python is often described as:

  • Powerful and fast to develop with — you can build useful programs with less code.
  • Friendly and easy to learn — its syntax is close to plain English.
  • Open — Python is open-source and free to use.
  • Cross-platform — the same Python code can usually run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
  • A team player — Python integrates well with databases, web services, C/C++ libraries, and other tools.

Python is a high-level language, meaning it hides many low-level computer details such as memory management and processor instructions. This makes development easier, though it may be slower than languages such as C or C++ for some performance-critical tasks.

Where Python Is Used

  • Python is not limited to one type of application. It is widely used for:
  • Desktop applications — GUI tools using Tkinter, PyQt, or Kivy.
  • Web applications — backend services using Django, Flask, and FastAPI.
  • Database applications — connecting to MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MongoDB, and other databases.
  • Network programming and scripting — automation, APIs, system administration, and network tools.
  • Data science, AI, and ML — data analysis, machine learning, deep learning, and prompt engineering workflows.
  • Automation — file handling, Excel automation, web scraping, testing, and task scheduling.

Python and Other Languages
Python “plays well with others” because it can connect with many technologies.

Implementation Works with Main idea
CPython C The standard/reference Python implementation; compiles Python to bytecode and runs it on a virtual machine. wikipedia
Cython C A Python superset that can compile Python-like code to C for better performance. wikipedia+1
Jython Java Runs Python on the Java platform. wiki.python
IronPython C# / .NET Runs Python on the .NET Common Language Runtime. wiki.python
PyPy Python An alternative implementation focused on faster execution. wiki.python

So, when people say “Python with C,” they often mean Cython or C extensions. “Python with Java” usually means Jython, and “Python with C#” means IronPython.

High-Level vs Low-Level Languages

A high-level language is easier for humans to read and write. Python, Java, and JavaScript are high-level languages.

A low-level language is closer to the hardware. It gives more control but is harder to write and maintain.

Feature High-level language Low-level language
Readability Easy Difficult
Hardware control Limited Strong
Development speed Fast Slower
Examples Python, Java Assembly, machine code

What Is Assembly Language?

Assembly language is a low-level language that uses short human-readable instructions such as MOV, ADD, and JMP. Each assembly instruction usually corresponds closely to a machine instruction.

Computers ultimately execute binary — sequences of 0s and 1s. Assembly is a step above binary because it uses readable names instead of raw numeric machine code.

Microprocessor vs Microservices

These terms sound similar but are completely different.

Term Meaning
Microprocessor A hardware chip that acts as the CPU of a computer or device.
Microservices A software architecture where an application is split into small, independent services.

For example, an e-commerce app may have separate microservices for users, payments, orders, and notifications. Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.

Python 2 vs Python 3

Python 2 and Python 3 are different major versions of Python. Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, and was intentionally not fully backward-compatible with Python 2.x.

Key differences include:

  • Python 3 uses print() as a function: print("Hello").
  • Python 3 handles Unicode text more naturally.
  • Integer division behaves differently: in Python 3, 5 / 2 gives 2.5.
  • Python 2 reached end of life on January 1, 2020

For any new project, use Python 3.

Python History and Major Releases

Version Release year Importance
Python 0.9.0 1991 First public release. developer.ibm
Python 1.0 1994 First major stable release. cvw.cac.cornell
Python 2.0 2000 Added major improvements such as list comprehensions and Unicode support. wikipedia
Python 3.0 2008 Major redesign; not fully compatible with Python 2. python
Python 2.7 2010 Final Python 2 release line; support ended in 2020. devguide.python

Python development began in December 1989, and the language has continued to evolve through regular Python 3 releases.

Interpreter and Compiler

Python is commonly called an interpreted language, but this is slightly simplified.

Compiler: Converts the entire source code into machine code or another lower-level form before execution.

Interpreter: Reads and executes code step by step.

CPython first compiles Python source code into bytecode, then executes that bytecode using the Python virtual machine. So Python uses both compilation and interpretation internally.

Backward Compatibility
Backward compatibility means that newer software can still run code written for an older version.

Python 3 was not fully backward-compatible with Python 2, which is why many older programs needed changes when moving from Python 2 to Python 3. However, within the Python 3.x series, most newer versions aim to remain compatible with earlier Python 3 code, with only occasional small changes.

Standalone and Task-Based Applications

A standalone application is a program that runs on a user’s device without needing a web browser. Python can create standalone desktop tools using GUI libraries and packaging tools such as PyInstaller.

A task-based application focuses on doing one specific job well, such as:

  • Automating Excel reports
  • Sending email notifications
  • Backing up files
  • Scraping product prices
  • Processing images
  • Running a machine-learning prediction

  • Web applications — backend services using Django, Flask, and FastAPI.
  • Database applications — connecting to MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MongoDB, and other databases.
  • Network programming and scripting — automation, APIs, system administration, and network tools.
  • Data science, AI, and ML — data analysis, machine learning, deep learning, and prompt engineering workflows.
  • Automation — file handling, Excel automation, web scraping, testing, and task scheduling.

Python and Other Languages
Python “plays well with others” because it can connect with many technologies.

Implementation Works with Main idea
CPython C The standard/reference Python implementation; compiles Python to bytecode and runs it on a virtual machine. wikipedia
Cython C A Python superset that can compile Python-like code to C for better performance. wikipedia+1
Jython Java Runs Python on the Java platform. wiki.python
IronPython C# / .NET Runs Python on the .NET Common Language Runtime. wiki.python
PyPy Python An alternative implementation focused on faster execution. wiki.python

So, when people say “Python with C,” they often mean Cython or C extensions. “Python with Java” usually means Jython, and “Python with C#” means IronPython.

High-Level vs Low-Level Languages

A high-level language is easier for humans to read and write. Python, Java, and JavaScript are high-level languages.

A low-level language is closer to the hardware. It gives more control but is harder to write and maintain.

Feature High-level language Low-level language
Readability Easy Difficult
Hardware control Limited Strong
Development speed Fast Slower
Examples Python, Java Assembly, machine code

What Is Assembly Language?

Assembly language is a low-level language that uses short human-readable instructions such as MOV, ADD, and JMP. Each assembly instruction usually corresponds closely to a machine instruction.

Computers ultimately execute binary — sequences of 0s and 1s. Assembly is a step above binary because it uses readable names instead of raw numeric machine code.

Microprocessor vs Microservices

These terms sound similar but are completely different.

Term Meaning
Microprocessor A hardware chip that acts as the CPU of a computer or device.
Microservices A software architecture where an application is split into small, independent services.

For example, an e-commerce app may have separate microservices for users, payments, orders, and notifications. Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.

Python 2 vs Python 3

Python 2 and Python 3 are different major versions of Python. Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, and was intentionally not fully backward-compatible with Python 2.x.

Key differences include:

  • Python 3 uses print() as a function: print("Hello").
  • Python 3 handles Unicode text more naturally.
  • Integer division behaves differently: in Python 3, 5 / 2 gives 2.5.
  • Python 2 reached end of life on January 1, 2020

For any new project, use Python 3.

Python History and Major Releases

Version Release year Importance
Python 0.9.0 1991 First public release. developer.ibm
Python 1.0 1994 First major stable release. cvw.cac.cornell
Python 2.0 2000 Added major improvements such as list comprehensions and Unicode support. wikipedia
Python 3.0 2008 Major redesign; not fully compatible with Python 2. python
Python 2.7 2010 Final Python 2 release line; support ended in 2020. devguide.python

Python development began in December 1989, and the language has continued to evolve through regular Python 3 releases.

Interpreter and Compiler

Python is commonly called an interpreted language, but this is slightly simplified.

Compiler: Converts the entire source code into machine code or another lower-level form before execution.

Interpreter: Reads and executes code step by step.

CPython first compiles Python source code into bytecode, then executes that bytecode using the Python virtual machine. So Python uses both compilation and interpretation internally.

Backward Compatibility
Backward compatibility means that newer software can still run code written for an older version.

Python 3 was not fully backward-compatible with Python 2, which is why many older programs needed changes when moving from Python 2 to Python 3. However, within the Python 3.x series, most newer versions aim to remain compatible with earlier Python 3 code, with only occasional small changes.

Standalone and Task-Based Applications

A standalone application is a program that runs on a user’s device without needing a web browser. Python can create standalone desktop tools using GUI libraries and packaging tools such as PyInstaller.

A task-based application focuses on doing one specific job well, such as:

  • Automating Excel reports
  • Sending email notifications
  • Backing up files
  • Scraping product prices
  • Processing images
  • Running a machine-learning prediction

title: Rulewright: A Smarter Way to Categorize Transactions with AI
summary:
Introducing Rulewright: A Smarter Way to Categorize Transactions

The Problem

Managing personal finances often means going through long lists of transactions from banks, UPI apps, and digital payment platforms. Categorizing every transaction manually can be repetitive and time-consuming.

I wanted to explore a simpler approach: what if transaction categorization could combine reusable rules with AI-powered suggestions while keeping the user in control?

That idea led me to build Rulewright.

What Is Rulewright?

Rulewright is a Python and Streamlit-based bookkeeping prototype that helps users categorize transaction records from CSV files.

The goal is to make transaction organization easier while allowing users to review suggestions before exporting their final ledger.

Key Features

1. CSV Transaction Import

Upload a CSV containing transaction descriptions and supported fields to get started. A fictional sample ledger is also available for testing.

2. Offline Categorization Rules

Create reusable merchant-based rules to categorize transactions without sending them to an AI service.

3. Gemini AI Suggestions

Rulewright can request category suggestions from the Google Gemini API. The suggested categories are drafts, not automatically approved financial records.

4. Human Review and Approval

Users can review and edit suggested categories, approve selected transactions, and inspect the final approved ledger before exporting it.

5. CSV and Rules Export

Download categorized transactions, approved records, and reusable rules for further work.

How It Works

The current workflow is straightforward:

  1. Upload a transaction CSV or load the fictional sample ledger.
  2. Define the categories you want to use.
  3. Generate offline rules or request AI suggestions.
  4. Review and edit the proposed categories.
  5. Approve the transactions you want to include.
  6. Download the resulting CSV.

Technology Stack

  • Python — application logic and transaction processing
  • Streamlit — interactive web interface
  • Pandas — CSV loading and tabular data processing
  • Google Gemini API — optional AI-powered category suggestions
  • Pytest — automated tests for core functionality

Privacy and Responsible AI

Financial transaction data can be sensitive. Rulewright includes a warning that transaction descriptions are sent to an external service when Gemini suggestions are requested.

For testing, I recommend using fictional data rather than real bank statements. Offline categorization is available without sending transaction descriptions to Gemini.

AI suggestions should always be reviewed before being treated as final financial records.

What I Learned

Building Rulewright helped me explore CSV processing, reusable categorization rules, API integration, data validation, approval workflows, and automated testing.

It also reinforced an important principle: AI can help make repetitive tasks easier, but users should remain in control of decisions involving their financial data.

Try Rulewright

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/LaxmikanthJanardhan01/rulewright
  • Live demo: https://rulewright-vzkikduphnnvksu7vgzouu.streamlit.app

What's Next?

I plan to improve the dashboard design, make transaction review more intuitive, strengthen CSV handling, and continue testing the application with fictional transaction data.

Rulewright is a prototype, and there is still plenty of room to improve it.

I'd love to hear your feedback: What feature would make a transaction categorization tool more useful to you?

Thanks for reading!

title: Tev plays Dino
summary:
I had, in a moment I can only call optimism, installed a small “decision model” called tev1 via Ollama. Tev1 is a family of open-weight, Jev-inspired decision and text-classification models released by Together AI and available in 4B and 0.8B parameter sizes fine-tuned from Qwen3.5.

If you are hearing about Jev for the first time - it is a chat-less, pick-more kinda LLM model. “Unlike standard conversational language models that output free-form text, Tev1 takes a structured input state, a question, and 2 to 24 labeled options, returning a specific option choice and probability distribution”. And it picks one, like a man at a buffet who has already decided on the fish.

Naturally I pointed it at the Chrome dino game. Its only natural because my official laptop’s official game-allowances only allow for a Chrome browser. The dino, you’ll recall, has one job: jump, duck, or stand there like a chump. A 4B model seemed exactly qualified for a job with three possible wrong answers.

Next, Claude rigged Playwright to drive the actual game and feed tev1 the details each time trouble approached: a cactus here, a pterodactyl there, going this fast. Whatever it said, jump or duck or nothing, the dino did. If it ducked a cactus, it ducked the cactus, and paid for it in full.

Results were mixed - it once ducked a pterodactyl skimming along at ground level, the exact sort you’re meant to leap over, with the confidence of a man backing his car with confidence after a few too many beer. The dino hasn’t, to date, broken the 2000 points ceiling. It has, however, broken several personal records for dying in novel ways. Improvement to its reaction-time will follow soon and code is here.

Originally published at visualist.in.

title: Lazy Notes: Let Local AI Do the Reading for You
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Ever opened a long meeting transcript or a pile of lecture notes and wished someone would just tell you what matters?

That's why I built Lazy Notes — a lightweight AI-powered note summarizer that helps people spend less time reading and more time doing.

Users can paste their notes or upload a text file and generate:

  • Quick Summary: Understand the main idea without reading every line.
  • Key Takeaways: Get the important points in bullet form.
  • Action Items: Identify tasks and deadlines mentioned in the notes.
  • Two-Line Recap: Get the essential information at a glance.

The idea is simple: let AI handle the repetitive reading so you don't have to.

Demo

Code

💻 GitHub Repository:

ansh-rajpoot / lazy-noted

The project is built with Python and Streamlit, with Ollama powering local AI inference.

How I Built It

I used Python, Streamlit, and Ollama to build Lazy Notes.

Streamlit provides the user interface, while Ollama runs an open-weight language model locally to process the notes and generate structured summaries.

The workflow is straightforward:

  1. The user pastes notes or uploads a supported text file.
  2. The application sends the text to the locally running Ollama model.
  3. The model generates a summary, key takeaways, and action items.
  4. The results are displayed in a clean interface that is easy to read and use.

I kept the architecture simple and focused on building a useful tool rather than adding unnecessary complexity.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that processes personal notes, meeting discussions, and study material, where the data goes matters.

Using a locally running open-weight model means Lazy Notes can process text without relying on a paid, third-party AI API.

This approach offers several advantages:

  • More control over data: Notes can remain on the user's machine when Ollama is configured locally and no other external services are used.
  • Model flexibility: Users can experiment with different compatible models instead of being locked into one hosted AI provider.
  • Lower ongoing costs: Local inference does not require paying a per-request AI API fee, although hardware and electricity still have costs.
  • More independence: The core summarization workflow can run without an internet connection once the required model is installed, provided the local setup is working.

Open innovation makes it possible to build a practical AI tool that users can run and control themselves.

The Lazy Payoff

The goal of Lazy Notes is to reduce the effort involved in reviewing long notes.

Instead of manually searching for the main ideas, users can start with a concise summary and review the details that matter to them.

I designed this project around one question:

What if getting the gist of your notes took less effort than reading them all?

title: Eight pre-registered tests on U.S. power plants that slip a month: what held, and what I take back
summary:
EIA's monthly generator inventory, EIA-860M, lists generators planned to start next month. Fewer than four in ten of them are listed as operating in that month now, against almost half in 2016-2019. Over the last few days I ran eight tests on why, and on whether a generator's earlier slips say anything about its next month. Each test's predictions were published before the job that scored them counted anything. 27 of the 33 predictions held.

What still stands. Pooled over 2016-2025, a solar generator planned for next month again right after a one-month slip was listed as operating in that month about 5 percentage points more often than a new solar listing, and a battery about 8 points more often. For solar since 2022, a slip of 2-3 months has been a bad sign: 12.5 points worse than a one-month slip. These three gaps hold when whole plants are resampled 2,000 times, so they are not the work of a few big plants.

What I take back. In my last post I wrote that gas and wind go the other way, and a later test on 2020-2021 seemed to confirm it for wind. With whole plants resampled, the wind and gas gaps are within plant-to-plant noise in every period. The same is true for all technologies together: a one-month slip is not shown to be a good sign on its own. One test that weighted each plant once failed two predictions, and the reason was the method, not the plants: that weighting lifts every repeat-listing group by construction.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • These are generator-months, and "on time" means the next monthly file lists the generator as operating. Resampling plants handles dependence inside a plant, not between plants of one developer or region. These are rates for groups, not forecasts for one generator.
  • The next test is the first on months that do not exist yet: October to December 2026, fixed before EIA publishes its October file on 24 November.

The summary note with every prediction and outcome, the code, the raw output and the tests that check every number are here: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.

title: Multi-Class Log Loss Explained: Math, MLE & Python Code
summary:
A comprehensive technical guide to Multi-Class Logarithmic Loss (Log Loss / Categorical Cross-Entropy): why lower loss indicates superior probabilistic calibration, how Maximum Likelihood Estimation requires the negative sign, why logarithms prevent floating-point underflow on large datasets, and how asymmetric penalties punish overconfident mispredictions.

1 · The Mathematical Formula & Variable Definitions

For a dataset containing N samples evaluated across C mutually exclusive classes, Multi-Class Logarithmic Loss is defined as:

$$L = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^C y_{i,c} \ln(p_{i,c})$$

Every symbol and variable in this formulation serves a distinct mathematical role:

Symbol / Variable Domain / Value Formal Definition & Mathematical Purpose
N Positive integer Total number of observations or samples in the evaluation dataset.
C Integer $\ge 2$ Total number of discrete candidate classes in the classification task.
y_{i,c} {0, 1} Binary one-hot indicator: equals 1 if observation i belongs to class c, and 0 otherwise.
p_{i,c} (0.0, 1.0) Model's predicted probability that observation i belongs to class c, where $\sum_c p_{i,c} = 1.0$.
\ln Mathematical operator The natural logarithm (base $e \approx 2.71828$). In information theory, base 2 is often used, measuring loss in bits.

2 · Why is Lower Better?

In statistical learning, loss functions quantify the divergence between prediction and reality. Multi-class log loss is strictly lower is better due to two fundamental conventions:

  • The Target Value (Zero Loss): A theoretically perfect model assigns a probability of exactly 1.0 to the true class and 0.0 to all other classes. Because $\ln(1.0) = 0$, the resulting log loss for a perfect prediction is exactly 0.0. As predictions become less certain or more erroneous, the loss value grows toward positive infinity.
  • Minimization Convention in Optimization: Machine learning algorithms (such as stochastic gradient descent, Adam, or tree splitting criteria) are designed to minimize an objective cost function. Formulating log loss so that 0 represents perfection allows standard gradient descent algorithms to iteratively step downhill toward minimum error.

3 · Why the Negative Sign? From MLE to Gradient Descent

The negative sign at the front of the formula is required by the mathematical relationship between probabilities and logarithms:

  • Probabilities are Fractions Less Than or Equal to 1: Valid probabilities p satisfy $0 < p \le 1$. The natural logarithm of any fraction between 0 and 1 is strictly negative (for example, $\ln(0.5) \approx -0.693$, and $\ln(0.1) \approx -2.302$).
  • Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): In classical statistics, generative and discriminative models are trained by maximizing the likelihood of observing the training data: $\max \prod_i P(y_i \mid x_i)$. Taking the natural logarithm converts this into maximizing the log-likelihood: $\max \sum_i \ln(P(y_i \mid x_i))$.
  • Flipping Maximization into Minimization: Because log-likelihood is negative, multiplying by -1 flips the sign from negative to positive. Maximizing the positive likelihood of the data is mathematically identical to minimizing the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL). The negative sign transforms statistical MLE into a convex loss surface that gradient descent can minimize.

4 · Why the Need for a Logarithm?

The logarithm is not an arbitrary mathematical choice; it solves two practical challenges in computation and model calibration:

1. Converting Products into Sums (Preventing Numerical Underflow)

Assuming independent data points, the joint probability of an entire dataset is the product of individual probabilities:

$$P_{\text{joint}} = P_1 \times P_2 \times \dots \times P_N$$

When multiplying thousands of floating-point numbers smaller than 1.0 (such as $0.8^{1000}$), the result approaches zero so quickly that standard 64-bit IEEE floating-point numbers experience arithmetic underflow (the computer rounds the value to absolute zero).

Applying the logarithm exploits the logarithmic identity $\ln(a \cdot b) = \ln(a) + \ln(b)$. This transforms product chains into numerically stable sums of negative numbers that CPUs can accumulate without precision loss.

2. Penalty Amplification for Overconfident Mistakes

The logarithmic curve acts as an asymmetric penalty amplifier. Because $\lim_{p \to 0} \ln(p) = -\infty$, the loss penalty escalates steeply as the predicted probability for the true class approaches zero:

Predicted Probability for True Class p_{true} Instance Log Loss Penalty -\ln(p_{true}) Practical Model Diagnosis
0.99 0.01005 Near-perfect prediction with high confidence.
0.80 0.22314 Accurate prediction with moderate certainty.
0.50 0.69315 Uncertain coin-flip assignment.
0.10 2.30259 Significant error: model favored alternative classes.
0.01 4.60517 Severe mistake: model was 99% confident in wrong classes.
0.0001 9.21034 Catastrophic penalty: one such prediction can wreck a batch average.

5 · Worked Numerical Example: 3-Class Animal Classifier

Consider a 3-class image classification model evaluating an image containing a Cat across three possible categories: [Cat, Dog, Bird].

  • True Ground Truth Label: y = [1, 0, 0] (Class 0 is Cat).
  • Baseline Model Prediction: p = [0.80, 0.10, 0.10].

Applying the multi-class formula for this single sample:

$$\text{Loss} = - [ 1 \cdot \ln(0.80) + 0 \cdot \ln(0.10) + 0 \cdot \ln(0.10) ]$$
$$\text{Loss} = - [ -0.22314 + 0 + 0 ] = \mathbf{0.22314}$$

Now consider two alternative prediction scenarios on the exact same sample:

Scenario A: High-Confidence Correct Prediction

The model predicts P(Cat) = 0.95, P(Dog) = 0.03, P(Bird) = 0.02:

$$\text{Loss} = -\ln(0.95) \approx \mathbf{0.05129} \quad (\text{Lower is better})$$

Scenario B: Confident Mistake (Misclassified as Dog)

The model erroneously predicts that the animal is a Dog with 90% confidence, leaving only P(Cat) = 0.05:

$$\text{Loss} = -\ln(0.05) \approx \mathbf{2.99573} \quad (\text{Over 13x higher penalty than baseline})$$

Because the logarithm curves sharply toward infinity near zero, a single confident misprediction in Scenario B produces a penalty larger than twenty accurate predictions combined.

6 · Robust Python Implementation (NumPy & PyTorch)

In software engineering, implementing -np.log(p) directly is dangerous: if the model outputs a probability of exactly 0.0, np.log(0.0) produces -inf, poisoning the entire dataset score with NaN. To prevent this, standard implementations clip probabilities by an epsilon threshold (typically 1e-15):

import numpy as np

def multiclass_log_loss(y_true, y_pred, eps=1e-15):
    # Clip probabilities to [eps, 1 - eps]
    y_pred_clipped = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1.0 - eps)

    # Renormalize rows so probabilities sum strictly to 1.0

1 · The Mathematical Formula & Variable Definitions

For a dataset containing N samples evaluated across C mutually exclusive classes, Multi-Class Logarithmic Loss is defined as:

$$L = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^C y_{i,c} \ln(p_{i,c})$$

Every symbol and variable in this formulation serves a distinct mathematical role:

N Positive integer Total number of observations or samples in the evaluation dataset.
C Integer $\ge 2$ Total number of discrete candidate classes in the classification task.
y_{i,c} {0, 1} Binary one-hot indicator: equals 1 if observation i belongs to class c, and 0 otherwise.
p_{i,c} (0.0, 1.0) Model's predicted probability that observation i belongs to class c, where $\sum_c p_{i,c} = 1.0$.
\ln Mathematical operator The natural logarithm (base $e \approx 2.71828$). In information theory, base 2 is often used, measuring loss in bits.

2 · Why is Lower Better?

In statistical learning, loss functions quantify the divergence between prediction and reality. Multi-class log loss is strictly lower is better due to two fundamental conventions:

  • The Target Value (Zero Loss): A theoretically perfect model assigns a probability of exactly 1.0 to the true class and 0.0 to all other classes. Because $\ln(1.0) = 0$, the resulting log loss for a perfect prediction is exactly 0.0. As predictions become less certain or more erroneous, the loss value grows toward positive infinity.
  • Minimization Convention in Optimization: Machine learning algorithms (such as stochastic gradient descent, Adam, or tree splitting criteria) are designed to minimize an objective cost function. Formulating log loss so that 0 represents perfection allows standard gradient descent algorithms to iteratively step downhill toward minimum error.

3 · Why the Negative Sign? From MLE to Gradient Descent

The negative sign at the front of the formula is required by the mathematical relationship between probabilities and logarithms:

  • Probabilities are Fractions Less Than or Equal to 1: Valid probabilities p satisfy $0 < p \le 1$. The natural logarithm of any fraction between 0 and 1 is strictly negative (for example, $\ln(0.5) \approx -0.693$, and $\ln(0.1) \approx -2.302$).
  • Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): In classical statistics, generative and discriminative models are trained by maximizing the likelihood of observing the training data: $\max \prod_i P(y_i \mid x_i)$. Taking the natural logarithm converts this into maximizing the log-likelihood: $\max \sum_i \ln(P(y_i \mid x_i))$.
  • Flipping Maximization into Minimization: Because log-likelihood is negative, multiplying by -1 flips the sign from negative to positive. Maximizing the positive likelihood of the data is mathematically identical to minimizing the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL). The negative sign transforms statistical MLE into a convex loss surface that gradient descent can minimize.

4 · Why the Need for a Logarithm?

The logarithm is not an arbitrary mathematical choice; it solves two practical challenges in computation and model calibration:

1. Converting Products into Sums (Preventing Numerical Underflow)

Assuming independent data points, the joint probability of an entire dataset is the product of individual probabilities:

$$P_{\text{joint}} = P_1 \times P_2 \times \dots \times P_N$$

When multiplying thousands of floating-point numbers smaller than 1.0 (such as $0.8^{1000}$), the result approaches zero so quickly that standard 64-bit IEEE floating-point numbers experience arithmetic underflow (the computer rounds the value to absolute zero).

title: I don't listen to meetings anymore. My sloth does.
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Taking notes in a meeting is expensive. While you're writing down what someone just said, you're already missing what they're saying now, so you end up doing two things badly. And most transcription and note-taking tools send the audio to someone else's server. In a lot of workplaces, mine included, that alone rules them out.

Durmain fixes that for me. It's a sloth that sleeps in the corner of the screen and listens to the call locally. When the call ends, it writes the minutes: a summary, the decisions, the tasks and who they belong to, and a score for how much the whole thing could have been an email.

And if I'm feeling too lazy to pay attention at all, that's fine too. The sloth wakes up and starts taking notes whenever someone says my name, so I know when I'm being pulled in.

Everything runs on my laptop. No audio and no text ever leave it.

Demo

The whole video was recorded with Wi-Fi off. The voice is a friend reading a fake meeting about a barbecue.

Code

breno-concrete / durmain

A sloth that sleeps in the corner of your screen during calls and wakes up when someone says your name. 100% local: faster-whisper + Ollama.

   

Durmain

A sloth that sleeps in the corner of your screen during calls and lectures,
wakes up when someone says your name, and writes the minutes when it's over.
Everything runs on your machine. No audio or text ever leaves it.

Why

Some meetings only need you for the thirty seconds when someone asks you something. The rest of the time you're half listening, and that's exactly when your name gets called.

Durmain listens to your computer's audio, transcribes it locally, and stays asleep until your name comes up. Then it wakes up, shows what was just said, and starts taking notes. When the call ends, a local LLM turns the transcript into minutes: a summary, decisions, tasks, every time you were mentioned, and an honest score for "this could have been an email".

Meeting audio is other people's voices and other people's words. It shouldn't go to a third-party…


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The open-source AI here is Whisper (open weights, through faster-whisper) for speech-to-text and Qwen2.5 7B (open weights, Apache 2.0) running locally through Ollama for the minutes.

The pipeline is simple:

system audio ─► 5 s blocks ─► faster-whisper + VAD ─► transcript
                                      │                    │
                                      ▼                    ▼ when the call ends
                              name detector ─► sloth   Ollama (qwen2.5:7b) ─► minutes
  • Capture: pyaudiowpatch records what the PC is playing (WASAPI loopback), in 5 second blocks.
  • Transcription: faster-whisper, model small, on CPU with int8. It runs on its own thread, with a queue between recording and transcribing, so recording never waits.
  • Name detection: rapidfuzz, word by word, because Whisper almost never writes my name the same way twice.
  • The sloth: a borderless tkinter window, always on top, with 20 animation frames.
  • Minutes: Ollama running qwen2.5:7b, only after the call ends. Never at the same time as the transcription.

That's the plan. Here's what actually happened.

Whisper makes things up when nobody is talking

The first time I paused a video, the transcript said "Legendas pela comunidade Amara.org" ("Subtitles by the Amara.org community"). Whisper learned from subtitled videos, so silence turns into subtitle credits. vad_filter=True wasn't enough on its own. I also drop segments with low confidence and filter a short list of known phantom phrases. After that: zero invented sentences during silence.

Ctrl+C stopped working

WASAPI loopback doesn't deliver any audio while nothing is playing. So stream.read() just sits there, blocked inside C code, and Python can't handle Ctrl+C until it returns. I moved the read to another thread. Ctrl+C worked, but closing the stream with that thread still stuck in read() gave me a segmentation fault. The fix was callback mode: PortAudio calls my function when there's audio, and nobody is ever stuck waiting.

Whisper can't spell my name

In my first scripted test, Whisper wrote "Brenna", "Brena", "Bruno" and "branco". The fuzzy match was fine. It just never got the right word.

Lowering the similarity threshold from 85 to 80 would catch "Bruno". But then every real Bruno in the meeting would wake the sloth, and my test script had Bruno and Brenda in it on purpose. Instead, I passed my name to Whisper as a hotword, which makes it more likely to pick that word when the audio is ambiguous.

Same recording, 20 mentions of my name and 6 decoy sentences: 15/20 became 16/20, still with 0 false alarms. It fixed the misspellings without turning the real Bruno into Breno.

The model copied my example

The prompt for the minutes took more rounds than any piece of code. A 7B model takes everything literally:

  • I put an example task in the prompt. The model listed that exact sentence as something that was said in the meeting.
  • I wrote "if the score is below 5, write 'not applicable'". It gave a 10/10 and wrote "not applicable".
  • I added a list of phrases that usually mean a task. It started marking everything as a task, including a compliment.

What worked: a template with no real-looking examples, no conditional rules, quotes copied from a single line of the transcript, and one rule I like a lot: when in doubt, don't list it. A missing item is better than an invented one.

The model thought I was talking

The early minutes said things like "Breno mentioned that...". But loopback only captures what comes out of the speakers, not my microphone. Every word in the transcript is someone else's. That limitation became a rule in the prompt: the user only listens.

Don't ask the LLM what code can do

I asked the model to list every time my name was mentioned. It found 6 out of 14. The name detector already had all 14, so now that section is built by code and the LLM never touches it. Use the LLM only where you actually need one.

The context window that cuts silently

A 20-minute lecture turned into 5,091 tokens. That's more than Ollama's default context window, and when that happens it doesn't throw an error. It just reads the beginning. Setting num_ctx to 16384 fixed it, but I only found out because I printed the token count.

The GPU crash

Once, right after a session, Ollama failed to load the model on my GPU with a CUDA error. Since the transcript is written to disk line by line during the call, nothing was lost. I ran the minutes script again and it worked.

This is what the CPU looks like during a live session. Every spike is one 5 second block going through Whisper:

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Meeting audio is other people's voices. They agreed to join a meeting, not to have their voice sent to a server I don't control. With open models running locally, that question doesn't even come up.

It also means it works offline (the demo was recorded with Wi-Fi off), it costs nothing per minute, and switching to another model is changing one string.

To be honest about the trade-off: a big closed model would probably do a better job on the minutes. In my test it would likely have caught the task Whisper half cut off, and it wouldn't file a decision as a task. That's what I give up. What I get is that nothing leaves my laptop, and I can read every line of what the tool does with the data. For meetings, I'll take that trade.

My Agent Session

I built this with an AI coding assistant acting as a mentor: it explained concepts and reviewed my code, and wrote some of the glue code (the Ollama call, the overlay) so I could make the deadline.

The Lazy Payoff

This week I used it on a 20-minute public lecture and on a test call with a friend. Writing those minutes by hand would take me 15 minutes; Durmain did it in under a minute.

What Result
Name detection, live call 8/10 mentions, 0 false alarms
Name detection, scripted recording 16/20, 0 false alarms
Alert latency 2.5 s on average (worst case ~7 s)
Minutes 8/10 decisions and tasks captured, 0 invented
20-minute lecture 5,091 tokens, minutes in ~36 s
Silence 0 invented sentences
Resources 583 MB of RAM, CPU spikes to ~40-50% for 1-2 s per block

It's not perfect. Blocks don't overlap, so a word spoken right at the edge of a block can get cut, and that caused most of the missed mentions. The 7B model sometimes puts things in the wrong section. Those are the next things I'd fix.

But for the meetings where I only need to hear my name, the sloth is already doing the listening.

title: RAG Chunking Done Right: Split on Structure, Attach Metadata, and Measure Recall Before You Touch chunk_size
summary:
When a RAG system gives a wrong answer, most people go straight for the model or the prompt. In my experience, the cause is often upstream: the right passage was never retrieved, because the chunk that held it was cut in the wrong place, was too big to rank well, or had lost the context that made it findable.

Chunking is the first step of almost every RAG pipeline, and it's the one people think about least. This post is the practical version: the trade-off you're actually tuning, what overlap does and doesn't buy you, why I split on document structure instead of fixed character counts, why every chunk should carry metadata, and how to measure recall before changing anything.

(Earlier posts covered hybrid search, lost in the middle, and long context vs RAG. This one sits one step before all of them: what goes into the index in the first place.)

1. Chunk size is a precision vs. context trade-off

There's no universally "right" chunk size, because two forces pull in opposite directions:

  • Small chunks are precise. Each embedding represents one idea, so a focused query matches it cleanly and you send fewer irrelevant tokens to the model. But a small chunk can lose the context it needs to make sense on its own.
  • Large chunks keep context together, but they dilute the embedding with unrelated content and fill your context window with tokens the model doesn't need.

Chroma's research team measured this directly in their report Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval. They evaluated retrieval at the token level (recall, precision and IoU) across five corpora and found that some chunking strategies outperformed others by up to 9% in recall. Some results worth knowing:

  • With text-embedding-3-large and 5 retrieved chunks, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter at 200 tokens with no overlap scored 88.1% recall and 7.0% precision. At 800 tokens with 400 overlap, recall was 85.4% and precision 1.5%.
  • They wrote that the heuristic recursive splitter at chunk size 200 with no overlap "performs well" and was consistently high across all their metrics.
  • They also noted that default settings of popular chunkers can perform relatively poorly. OpenAI's file search default (800-token chunks, 400-token overlap) gave slightly below-average recall and the lowest scores on their other metrics in that setup.

The speculation in that report matches what I see in practice: recall peaks somewhere in the middle. Too large and the relevant sentence is diluted; too small and the chunk doesn't carry enough context to be retrieved as one unit.

Know your defaults, because you're probably using one:

Tool Default / documented setting
OpenAI vector stores (file search) 800-token chunks, 400-token overlap; configurable from 100 to 4096 tokens, overlap at most half the chunk size (docs)
